newsReadings.passage:
Detecting trace chemicals in the air — the faint odour of explosives, the invisible leak of a toxic gas, the first molecular whisper of disease — has long been one of technology's most stubborn challenges. Synthetic sensors, for all their precision, struggle in real-world environments where hundreds of compounds mingle and interfere. Evolution, however, has been refining chemical detection for hundreds of millions of years. A team of researchers has now shown that the most powerful sensor may be a hybrid: a living insect, augmented with nanomaterials, that outperforms both biology and machines alone.

The insect in question is the locust, whose antennae are studded with tens of thousands of olfactory receptors capable of discerning minute differences between odorants. Working with Srikanth Singamaneni's laboratory, which specialises in designing and synthesising nanomaterials, and Barani Raman's group, which has spent years mapping the locust's sensory circuits, the researchers attached a specially engineered foam to the insect's antennae. The foam is built from plasmonic nanostructures — metallic architectures that concentrate light into intense electromagnetic hotspots, enabling a technique known as surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, or SERS, which can identify individual molecules by their vibrational fingerprints.

The crucial finding was that the foam augmented the locust's odour-detecting abilities without interfering with its other functions. In a series of tests, the hybrid systems successfully detected a wider range of smells than both unmodified locusts and state-of-the-art synthetic chemical sensors. Remarkably, the biohybrid detectors picked up the chemical signature of TNT, the explosive, demonstrating a sensitivity that could have immediate applications in security screening and environmental monitoring.

The collaboration itself illustrates how modern science increasingly advances at the boundaries between disciplines. Singamaneni's laboratory has spent years perfecting the design and synthesis of plasmonic nanostructures, materials whose optical properties can be tuned with extraordinary precision. Raman's team, meanwhile, has devoted equal effort to mapping the neural circuitry that carries signals from the locust's antennae to its brain, work that revealed just how sophisticated the insect's odour-processing machinery already is. Bringing these two lines of enquiry together was not simply a matter of sticking a material onto an insect: the foam had to be engineered to interface with the antenna without obstructing the sensory hairs through which odours reach the receptors. That the researchers succeeded — and that the resulting system outperformed both non-SERS locusts and synthetic sensors across every chemical tested — suggests the approach is robust rather than a laboratory curiosity.

What makes this achievement significant is not merely the raw performance but the way two fundamentally different detection strategies complement each other. The biological component — the locust's antenna — provides exquisite selectivity and the ability to operate in complex, noisy chemical environments, a feat that artificial sensors find notoriously difficult. The nanomaterial component adds a second, independent mode of detection, allowing researchers to confirm and characterise what the insect senses. As Raman observed, the results clearly showed that the best of the two worlds can be merged.

A key challenge in chemical sensing, Raman noted, is that researchers often do not know in advance which molecules they are targeting. A sensor tuned for one compound may be blind to another. The foam attached to the antenna helps identify particular chemical species, adding analytical power to the insect's broad-spectrum awareness. The biology and the chemical sensing parts complement each other: where the locust detects that something is present, the plasmonic foam helps determine precisely what it is.

The implications extend well beyond the laboratory. Biohybrid sensors of this kind could one day be deployed for detecting explosives at checkpoints, monitoring industrial emissions, or even diagnosing disease from breath samples — all tasks where detecting minute chemical traces reliably and inexpensively remains a formidable obstacle. The research, published in the journal Advanced Materials under the title "Plasmonic Foam-Enabled Dual-Modal Biohybrid Chemical Sensor," suggests that the future of sensing may lie not in choosing between nature and engineering, but in the deliberate fusion of the two.

newsReadings.passage:
Global warming driven by fossil fuel emissions is not merely continuing — it is accelerating, pushing many of the Earth's most important ecosystems towards the brink. That was the stark warning delivered by Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, at the Reuters Sustainability Europe conference in London on Tuesday, just weeks before the United Nations' COP31 climate talks open on 9 November.

Rockström told delegates that damage to coral reefs and the Amazon rainforest was approaching a point where it could become irreversible. Even parts of the Atlantic Ocean circulation system — including the current that carries warm water from the Caribbean and moderates Western Europe's climate — were close to collapse, he said. These systems are among the planet's critical tipping points: thresholds beyond which change becomes self-reinforcing and cannot be undone.

To understand why Rockström's warning carries such weight, it helps to grasp what scientists mean by a tipping point. Most environmental change is gradual: a little more warming produces a little more damage. A tipping point breaks this pattern. Once crossed, the change becomes self-reinforcing — a forest that once absorbed carbon begins to release it as trees die, or melting ice exposes darker water that absorbs still more heat. The system then continues to deteriorate even if the original pressure is removed. Coral reefs, which support a quarter of all marine life despite covering a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, are acutely sensitive to even small rises in sea temperature; prolonged heat causes the corals to expel the symbiotic algae that sustain them, leaving behind bleached skeletons. The Amazon, meanwhile, generates much of its own rainfall through the moisture its trees release into the air — a cycle that begins to fail as deforestation and drought thin the forest canopy.

The latest science, Rockström added, confirms that the world is on course to exceed a 1.5 degree Celsius rise in average surface temperature within the next few years. Such a rise would intensify the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, from prolonged heatwaves to devastating floods, placing ever greater strain on communities and economies alike.

The 1.5 degree threshold Rockström referenced has become the defining benchmark of international climate policy. Adopted as an aspirational goal in the 2015 Paris Agreement, it was chosen because beyond it the risks of crossing multiple tipping points rise sharply. Exceeding it does not mean an overnight catastrophe, but it does mean entering a zone where extreme weather becomes markedly more frequent and where the margin for reversing course narrows with each passing year. For the delegates gathering at COP31 in November, Rockström's intervention sets an uncomfortable agenda: pledges made in conference halls must now be matched by the far harder work of rewiring energy systems, reforming subsidies, and defending the natural systems that ultimately underwrite human prosperity.

Addressing business leaders, Rockström argued that companies preparing for this future should treat climate and nature as a single integrated agenda rather than managing them separately. While continuing to prioritise efforts to decarbonise their operations, firms should also invest in preserving nature — particularly projects aimed at rebuilding biodiversity and protecting reserves of fresh water, both of which buffer societies against climate shocks.

He reserved his sharpest criticism for political backsliding. Rockström said it was "incredibly disturbing" to witness lobbying for an easing of regulations designed to phase out internal combustion engine vehicles. Subsidies for petrol and diesel, he argued, were actively undermining consumer demand for electric vehicles at precisely the moment when momentum needed to accelerate. The message was unambiguous: the science is clear, the risks are compounding, and delay is no longer a neutral choice — it is a decision whose costs will be measured in ecosystems lost and lives disrupted.

newsReadings.passage:
For the millions of people worldwide who rely on cochlear implants to hear, technological progress has traditionally arrived through the device worn behind the ear. The internal implant — the component placed surgically inside the head — has remained essentially fixed from the day of the operation. A newly recognised innovation promises to change that paradigm, bringing the concept of the software update to the implant itself.

Cochlear Limited, a global leader in implantable hearing solutions, announced this week that its Nucleus Nexa System has been named one of TIME's Best Inventions of 2026. Described as the world's first and only smart cochlear implant system, the Nexa platform was nominated by TIME's editors, who solicited nominations from correspondents around the world alongside direct applications, paying particular attention to growing fields such as health care and artificial intelligence.

The core breakthrough lies in the implant's upgradeable firmware. Traditionally, innovation in cochlear implants has been delivered almost entirely through the external sound processor, while the implanted component remained unchanged after surgery. The Nexa System breaks with this constraint by building smart, upgradeable technology directly into the implant. Future advances in signal processing can therefore be delivered through both the implant and the sound processor, rather than the external unit alone.

According to Dig Howitt, CEO and President of Cochlear, the system was designed from the outset not merely for the technology of today but for the possibilities of tomorrow. By allowing the implanted hardware to evolve, the platform opens up new possibilities for how cochlear implant technology can develop over time — a shift Howitt described as a source of considerable pride for the company, and, more importantly, of promising benefits for recipients in the years ahead.

Hearing loss is among the most common sensory disabilities in the world, affecting hundreds of millions of people and often isolating them from education, work, and social life. For those with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss, conventional hearing aids — which depend on residual function in the inner ear — offer limited help, making cochlear implants the only viable path to perceiving sound. Yet the decision to undergo implantation has always carried a quiet compromise: the internal device, once placed, could not keep pace with the rapid evolution of digital signal processing happening outside the body. Each generation of external processor brought clearer sound, but the implant's own capabilities remained frozen in time. The Nexa platform removes that compromise, aligning the lifespan of the implanted hardware with the far faster rhythm of software innovation.

The significance of the advance becomes clearer when one considers how a cochlear implant works. Unlike a hearing aid, which simply amplifies sound, a cochlear implant bypasses damaged parts of the inner ear and directly stimulates the auditory nerve with electrical signals. The external processor captures sound and converts it into digital instructions; the implant then translates those instructions into the intricate patterns of stimulation the brain learns to interpret as hearing. Improvements to either half of this chain can sharpen what a recipient perceives — which is why making the implanted half upgradeable matters so much.

For recipients, the practical implications are substantial. Children implanted at a young age may use the same internal device for decades; an upgradeable implant means they can benefit from each new iteration of processing technology without additional surgery. Audiologists, too, gain finer tools for calibrating devices to individual needs. Wider adoption of such platforms could accelerate a virtuous cycle: as the installed base of smart implants grows, the incentive to develop ever more sophisticated processing algorithms grows with it.

The recognition by TIME places the Nexa System among the year's most celebrated innovations — a reminder that some of the most transformative technologies are not the ones that dazzle on a stage, but the ones that quietly extend human capability. For those whose world was once silent, an implant that can keep learning may mean a lifetime of hearing that keeps getting better.
